newsitem.title: TURKEY: Germany's Kinkel boosts Turkish rights workers.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kinkel boosts Turkish rights workers.

text.p: Visiting German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel gave moral support on Thursday to embattled Turkish activists investigating human rights, one of the main issues blocking Turkey's bid to join Europe.
Kinkel held separate talks in Ankara and Istanbul with human rights leaders who often face prosecution for their work in denouncing torture, illegal killings and "disappearances".
"He said he knows that (non-governmental organisations) NGOs are in a difficult situation in Turkey and said he supported our work," said Human Rights Association chairman Akin Birdal.

Birdal was one of four human rights workers who met Kinkel over breakfast at a five-star hotel in the capital. "He mentioned the human rights and Kurdish problems and the fact that they have not been solved," Birdal told Reuters.

Kinkel, on a two-day official visit, said on Wednesday that Turkey belongs in Europe but that its human rights performance and its treatment of the Kurdish minority were among several problems preventing Ankara from joining the European Union.

The European Parliament has blocked hundreds of millions of dollars in EU aid to Turkey in an attempt to get Ankara to clean up on rights. Many accusations of abuses come from the mainly Kurdish southeast where separatist rebels have been battling security forces for 12 years.

Pro-Kurdish journalists said rights workers in Istanbul had told Kinkel of a recent case of a civilian who had gone missing under suspicious circumstances from the southeastern city of Diyarbakir more than a month ago.
Rights group Amnesty International said in a report last October that more than 100 people, mostly Kurdish villagers, had disappeared in police custody since 1993.
Kinkel, a liberal, told journalists on a flight from Ankara to Istanbul that he had given Turkish counterpart Tansu Ciller a list of violations at a meeting on Wednesday.
He said Turkey's rights record gave "cause for concern".

Kinkel had been close to cancelling his visit because of media reports quoting Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan as urging him to repent in a dispute over a trade deal between Turkey and the European Union.
Turkey and some leading EU countries have been on a collision course since Ankara threatened in January to veto NATO's planned expansion if it were not given guarantees of eventual EU membership.

Moslem but secular Turkey has been an associate member of the EU since 1963. But the rights problem, economic woes and disputes with full member Greece have blocked its efforts to get closer to Europe.

Turkey has promoted a new detention law passed by parliament earlier this month as proof it is taking European concerns on rights seriously. The law cuts the maxiumum period of police custody to a week in most of the country.
But rights workers say police torture continues. "There has been no change in the inhuman treatment at detention centres," the Human Rights Association said in a statement.
